title: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Projection Transformation
To perform geoprocessing using two geospatial datasets, both datasets must be projected using the same coordinate reference system.

Update ESPG Code
This is used to correct missing or wrongly assigned coordinate system during the data import process.
To display currently assigned coordinate system:

st_crs(mpsz)

Coordinate Reference System:
  User input: WGS 84 
  wkt:
GEOGCRS["WGS 84",
    DATUM["World Geodetic System 1984",
        ELLIPSOID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563,
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]]],
    PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,
        ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
    CS[ellipsoidal,2],
        AXIS["geodetic latitude (Lat)",north,
            ORDER[1],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
        AXIS["geodetic longitude (Lon)",east,
            ORDER[2],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
    ID["EPSG",4326]]


The above indicates that EPSG is 4326 (degree of latitude or longtitude).
To change EPSG to 3414 (measure distance):

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)

title: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Convert to Spatial Object

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(listings, 
               coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
               crs=4326) %>%
st_transform(crs = 3414)

Note: coords - x = longitude and y = latitude in standard mapping convention.
crs - requires coordinates system in EPSG format. 4326 is wgs84 Geographic Coordinate System and EPSG: 3414 is Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System. %>% - nest st_transform() to transform the newly created simple feature data frame into svy21 projected coordinates system. (feed to next function)

title: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Geoprocessing with sf package

Use Case 1: Land Acquisition Analysis
Scenario: The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on the both sides of the existing cycling path. You are tasked to determine the extend of the land need to be acquired and their total area.
Solution:

Compute the 5-meter buffers around cycling paths.


buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)


buffer_cycling <- st_transform(buffer_cycling, 3414)


Calculate the area of the buffers:


buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)


Derive total land area impacted.


sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]



Create a plot to show the buffer by using a selected planning subzone (i.e. Tampine West).



Extract polygon feature of Tampines West:


mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST") 


Clip cycling buffers within Tampines West planning subzone.


buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
all geometries



Create the plot.


plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected))










Use Case 2: Determine Number of Preschools by Planning Subzone
Scenario: The authority requires a count of pre-schools for each Planning Subzone to support forward planning. Using R and the sf package, perform the necessary geoprocessing to compute these counts and present the results clearly.
Solution:

Identify and calculate number of preschools in each Planning Subzone:


mpsz$`PreSchool Count`<- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

Check summary statistics:

summary(mpsz$`PreSchool Count`)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    0.00    4.00    7.09   10.00   72.00 



List Planning Subzone with most preschools:

Derive area of each Planning Subzone:


mpsz$Area <- mpsz %>%
  st_area()


Compute Preschool Density:


mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(`PreSchool Density` = `PreSchool Count`/Area * 1000000)


Data Visualisation



Plot histogram to reveal distribution of Preschool Density. Basic histogram:



hist(mpsz$`PreSchool Density`)








Improved visuals:

ggplot(data=mpsz, 
       aes(x= as.numeric(`PreSchool Density`)))+
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue") +
  labs(title = "Are Preschools Evenly Distributed in Singapore?",
       subtitle= "There are many planning subzones with only 1 preschool and 7 planning subzones with at least 30 or more preschools",
      x = "Preschool Density (per km sq)",
      y = "Frequency")









Scatterplot to show relationship between Preschool Density and Preschool Count:


ggplot(data=mpsz, 
       aes(y = `PreSchool Count`, 
           x= as.numeric(`PreSchool Density`)))+
  geom_point(color="black", 
             fill="light blue") +
  xlim(0, 40) +
  ylim(0, 40) +
  labs(title = "",
      x = "Preschool Density (per km sq)",
      y = "Preschool Count")

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible (e.g. population, temperature, crime rate, property prices et cetera).
Geovisualisation is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyse, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Data Preparation
Prepare a data table with the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup()%>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by PA, SZ, and AG.
ℹ Output is grouped by PA and SZ.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(PA, SZ, AG))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.


Convert values in PA and SZ to uppercase:

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), 
          .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Join the geographical and attribute table using planning subzone name (SUBZONE_N and SZ) as the commmon identifier:

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

Note: Using left_join() ensurs the output will be a simple features data frame.

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Choropleth Mapping
Choropleth mapping involves the symbolisation of enumeration units, such as countries, provinces, states, counties or census units, using area patterns or graduated colors.

Plot Using qtm()
(+) Concise and provides good visuals in most cases

library(tmap)
tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`

qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










Plot Using tmap() elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Drawing a Base Map
tm_shape() is used to define the input data and tm_polygons() is used to draw the planning subzone polygons.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

Using tm_fill() only

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

Using tm_fill() and tm_borders()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

  tm_borders()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+

  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")

section: Plot Choropleth Map with Custom Break
text:
Plot Choropleth Map with Custom Break
The breakpoints can be set explicitly by means of the breaks argument to the tm_scale_intervals(). In tmap, the breaks include a minimum and maximum. n+1 elements must be specified in the breaks option to end up with n.
Descriptive statistics:

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1905  0.7450  0.8377  0.8738  0.9366 12.7500      94 


Plot map with breaks:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

Warning: Values have found that are higher than the highest break. They are
assigned to the highest interval

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
section: Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps (Facet Maps)
text:
Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps (Facet Maps)

Method 1: Assign multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning two variables to the visual variable (i.e. fill).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")

style set to "natural"


other available styles are: "white" (tmap default), "gray", "cobalt", "albatross", "beaver", "bw", "classic", "watercolor"


tmap v3 styles: "v3" (tmap v3 default), "gray_v3", "natural_v3", "cobalt_v3", "albatross_v3", "beaver_v3", "bw_v3", "classic_v3", "watercolor_v3"











Method 2: Arrange multiples choropleth maps in a grid layout
In this example, multiple choropleth maps are created and tmap_arrnage() is used to arrnage them in a grid layout.

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile", 
              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)










Method 3: Define a group-by variable in tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by using tm_facets().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Map Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion (Filter)
Select geographical area of interest and plot a choropleth map focus only on the selected region.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
section: Complement Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
text:
Complement Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Maps and statistical charts complement each other by visually representing different aspects of the same data, offering a more comprehensive understanding.
Maps excel at showing spatial relationships and geographical patterns, while charts effectively display numerical data, trends, and comparisons. Combining both allows for a more insightful and engaging data narrative, especially when dealing with spatial data that also has quantifiable characteristics.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








Improve visualisation:

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile", 
            values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(),
          fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

title: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Create Interactive Map
Interactive maps let users actively explore and interact with the data they display.
Unlike static maps, you can zoom in and out, pan across areas, click on locations for more information, and even work with data overlays or visualizations—making the experience more dynamic and informative.
One of the great things about tmap is that it lets you switch easily between static and interactive maps using tmap_mode(), so you can choose the view that best suits your analysis.
`By modifying the code chunk in sub-section 2.6, the code chunks below build an interactive map using

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)






Include Zoom function:

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))
